title: I Wrote Other Things That Are Not Funny
subtitle: A brief roundup of bylines across the internet!
body_html:
Owen Scott Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, is best known for his somewhat absurdist writing here on The Frontier Psychiatrists Newsletter.

It’s a health-themed newsletter so amusing that it has spawned a whole series of exciting live-action newsletter events! They are called “RAMHT” (short for Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment), and the next one is coming up on January 11th, 2026!

Join us at RAMHT-AI

However, I don’t only write here in this newsletter. Sometimes, I put on a tie, act like an adult, and write something palatable for my friends who work in roles with much more pressure from corporate comms teams and quarterly earnings calls.

For example, I wrote this for MedCity News:

Combining Ketamine and Deep TMS: A New Frontier in Treating Depression

“However, progress without equitable access? That is a hollow victory. Payment models and healthcare infrastructure have not kept pace with scientific breakthroughs. This is leaving too many patients behind. Our challenge, now, is to align science, policy, and clinical practice so that innovative therapies like ketamine and dTMS are available to the patients who need them most – when they need them.”

I sound so…professional! Dear readers, don’t worry, I was wearing low-top Chuck Taylors the whole time I was drafting that article.

Or how about my recent quotes in Everyday Health?

Huge Study on Antidepressant Side Effects Could Lead to More Personalized Prescribing

“Doctors typically start patients on lower doses, monitor side effects and effectiveness, and adjust the dose based on “response and tolerability,” says Owen Scott Muir, MD, a psychiatrist and chief medical officer at Radial, a psychiatric practice based in New York City, who was not involved with the research.”

I sound so…measured.

I’m making fun of myself, of course. I do think it’s worth understanding that not all writing serves the same purpose. Sometimes, we are trying to educate in a way that is easy to read and understand as physicians and writers. Other times, we are advocating to different audiences for policy change. Sometimes, we are trying to inspire.

I also wrote a few research papers that are now publicly available.

For example, this pivotal trial for the FDA clearance of Accelerated dTMS with the H1 coil, on which I was a coauthor, along with many others!

Accelerated Deep TMS for Depression: Results from a Multisite, Randomized Non-Inferiority Trial

I also did some light authoring in real-life presentations, such as:

Current Evidence Base of Transcutaneous Nerve Stimulation Treatments in Youth

And even engaged in a debate at the AACAP 2025 annual meeting:

Debate: Should High Schools Ban Smartphones?

I even contributed to an article over at the Carlat Report…

TMS, Teens, and Antidepressants

Regardless, learning to write well and in different genres is what makes a well-rounded writer. It’s been worth my time, and I hope reading what I have to share has been equally helpful to you, my dear readers.

To all my fellow writers—keep at it! It is an experiment in understanding our readers' minds and adjusting when our imagined audience differs from who we need to reach.

Thanks for following along. I have a few academic papers to get out the door, or I’d have more for you today!
